name: Selepressin
route: Continuous intravenous infusion in a hospital
status: Investigational and discontinued; the phase 2b/3 SEPSIS-ACT trial in septic shock was stopped for futility
mechanism: Activates vasopressin V1a receptors to tighten blood vessels while avoiding V2 receptors, aiming to raise pressure and limit fluid leakage in sepsis

article.summary: Selepressin is an experimental vasopressin-like drug that targets only V1a receptors. It was tested in septic shock, but the large SEPSIS-ACT trial was stopped for futility and it is not approved.
article.takeaway: Selepressin is an experimental, lab-made relative of vasopressin that activates only the V1a receptor, which tightens blood vessels. It was developed for septic shock in the hope of raising blood pressure while limiting the fluid leakage that makes sepsis worse. A small phase 2a trial suggested it could replace norepinephrine,[^1] but the 868-patient SEPSIS-ACT trial found no difference in ventilator- and vasopressor-free days (**15.0** vs **14.5**) and was stopped for futility.[^2] Selepressin is not FDA-approved.
glance: Continuous IV infusion titrated to blood pressure
Phase 2a (53 patients) and phase 2b/3 SEPSIS-ACT (868 patients)

blocks.text: Natural [vasopressin](/peptides/vasopressin) acts on three receptors: V1a on blood vessels, V1b in the pituitary and V2 in the kidney. Selepressin is a peptide analog built to act almost only on V1a. In sheep with severe sepsis it blocked vascular leak, the seepage of fluid from blood vessels that causes swelling and organ injury, and in a septic shock model it performed better than vasopressin or norepinephrine.[^3][^4]
The appeal was a non-catecholamine vasopressor. Norepinephrine, the first-line drug, is not always effective and has catecholamine side effects.[^2]

After a phase 2a study, Ferring Pharmaceuticals ran SEPSIS-ACT (NCT02508649), an adaptive phase 2b/3 trial that began in July 2015 at 63 hospitals in Belgium, Denmark, France, the Netherlands and the United States. It was stopped for futility at the end of its first part, and the registry lists it as terminated.[^2][^5] Development in septic shock has ended, and the drug has no approved use.

rows: At 2.5 ng/kg/min about 50% and 70% kept blood pressure up without norepinephrine at 12 and 24 hours; 7-day norepinephrine dose 249 vs 761 mcg/kg on placebo[^1]
868 randomized adults (828 treated) with septic shock needing more than 5 mcg/min of norepinephrine
Ventilator- and vasopressor-free days 15.0 vs 14.5 (P=0.30); 90-day deaths 40.6% vs 39.4%[^2]

blocks.text: Kidney-replacement-free days (18.5 vs 18.2) and ICU-free days (12.6 vs 12.2) were also similar. The two trials fit together: selepressin could hold up blood pressure, but doing so did not translate into more days free of ventilators or vasopressors or into better survival.[^2]

items: **In SEPSIS-ACT,** cardiac arrhythmias occurred in 27.9% on selepressin vs 25.2% on placebo, cardiac ischemia in 6.6% vs 5.6%, mesenteric (bowel) ischemia in 3.2% vs 2.6% and peripheral ischemia in 2.3% in both groups.[^2]

**In phase 2a,** the 2.5 ng/kg/min dose was well tolerated, with adverse events as frequent as on placebo. A higher dose group was stopped after one patient's infusion was discontinued for possible safety reasons.[^1]

blocks.text: Reduced blood flow to organs is the general concern with any strong vasoconstrictor, which is why ischemia was tracked closely.

SEPSIS-ACT's authors noted that further research would be needed to judge selepressin against other patient-centered outcomes,[^2] but the program was not continued. In current practice, guidelines recommend norepinephrine first and suggest adding vasopressin if blood pressure remains low.[^6]

evidence.label: Well tested, but the main trial found no benefit
evidence.text: Two randomized trials exist. The phase 2a trial showed a blood pressure effect,[^1] but the large phase 2b/3 trial found no improvement in clinical outcomes.[^2]

faq.a: No. Its main trial, SEPSIS-ACT, was stopped for futility, and the drug is no longer in development for septic shock.[^2][^5]

faq.q: How is it different from vasopressin?
faq.a: [Vasopressin](/peptides/vasopressin) activates V1a, V1b and V2 receptors. Selepressin was engineered to act almost only on V1a, hoping for a cleaner effect on blood vessels, but it did not show better outcomes in SEPSIS-ACT.[^2]

faq.q: Why did it fail if it raised blood pressure?
faq.a: Raising blood pressure with a drug does not automatically improve outcomes. Patients on selepressin had about the same number of ventilator- and vasopressor-free days (15.0 vs 14.5) as those on placebo.[^2]
